claims.text: The proposed framework integrates machine-learning-enhanced CALPHAD models with targeted experimental calibration.
The framework can predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The framework can achieve accuracy comparable to traditional DFT-based simulations.
The framework has significantly lower computational cost than traditional DFT-based simulations.
The intended initial materials are single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloys in their solid state at ambient pressure.
Machine learning can efficiently sample the relevant compositional and structural parameter space.
Limited experimental measurements can be used to calibrate the combined machine-learning and CALPHAD predictions.
The framework is primarily applicable at ambient pressure to alloys forming single-phase solid solutions without significant ordering or competing phase transitions.
Local atomic configurations and multielement interaction networks mediate the solid-to-liquid transition in high-entropy alloys.
The local configurations and multielement interaction networks underlie the high configurational entropy of these alloys.
The machine-learning model captures complex nonlinear relationships between alloy composition and fusion thermodynamics.
Using the learned composition-property relationships to inform CALPHAD enables more efficient free-energy calculations.
Machine-learning-assisted free-energy calculations reduce computational cost while preserving quantitative accuracy.
Calibration with limited experimental inputs refines predictions so that phase-change parameters reflect the underlying physical interactions.
Predicted melting temperatures and fusion properties will have relative errors of approximately 5–10% against full-scale DFT or experiments.
Predicted volume changes at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties will be accurate to approximately 5–10%.
Traditional DFT-based molecular dynamics and full-scale CALPHAD without machine-learning acceleration are more computationally intensive and less efficient across broad composition spaces.
The framework may have limited applicability to alloys with ordering, precipitation, other complex phase transformations, sparse calibration data, multiphase regions, or non-ambient conditions.
